title: Symphony No. 8 in G major
hook: A summer in the Bohemian countryside, with birdsong, a village band and trumpets that call to the dance.

painting.title: The Chrudimka Valley
painting.pairingNote: A Bohemian valley in high summer, meadow, haystack and woods, painted two years before Dvořák wrote this symphony in the Bohemian countryside.

facts: Dvořák wrote the symphony between 26 August and 8 November 1889, mostly at Vysoká, his summer house in the Bohemian countryside south-west of Prague. It was the place where he was most at ease, and the music is full of open air.

He had just been elected to the new Bohemian Academy of Sciences, Literature and Arts, and dedicated the score to it “in thanks for my election”. He wanted a symphony “different from the other symphonies”, with ideas “worked out in a new way”. His Seventh, four years earlier, had been dark and stormy; this one is sunny.

He conducted the first performance in Prague on 2 February 1890, and the London premiere that April. He wrote to a friend that the applause in London grew after every movement, until it was “almost unbearable”.

It was published in London by Novello, not by his usual publisher Simrock, after the two quarrelled over the fee. That is why it is sometimes called the “English” symphony, although nothing in it is English.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a hymn and a birdcall in the open fields (I), a slow movement of light and shadow (II), a wistful waltz (III), trumpets and a set of variations that ends in a whirl (IV).

movements.heading: Allegro con brio
movements.summary: The symphony is in G major, but it begins in G minor, with a warm, hymn-like melody for cellos and low winds. Then a flute takes off on a bright birdcall, and the major key arrives. That opening melody comes back like a signpost at the start of each new section: Dvořák builds a [[sonata-form|sonata form]] around it rather than around one main theme.

mainIdeas.name: The hymn
mainIdeas.description: a broad, songful G minor melody in cellos, clarinets, bassoons and horn, seventeen bars long, which drifts through other keys before landing on G major.

mainIdeas.name: The birdcall
mainIdeas.description: a light, chirping tune in the flute, rising and falling over soft strings.

mainIdeas.name: The second theme
mainIdeas.description: a dotted, dancing tune in the woodwinds, in B minor, that soon swells into a bright B major tutti.

stops.hear: A warm, singing melody low in the cellos and winds, with soft plucked basses below
stops.happening: The hymn-like opening, in G minor

stops.hear: A single flute takes off with a quick, chirping tune
stops.happening: The birdcall theme, and the key turns to G major

stops.hear: The whole orchestra bursts in with the flute’s tune, timpani ringing
stops.happening: The first big climax, very early

stops.hear: Woodwinds play a dotted, skipping tune in the minor, which grows into a bright, loud passage
stops.happening: The second group of themes, B minor turning to B major

stops.hear: The quiet hymn returns in the low strings, as at the very beginning
Fragments of the birdcall are tossed around; the music darkens and builds into a storm
stops.happening: The stormiest part of the movement

stops.hear: At the top of the storm, the trumpets blare out the hymn
stops.happening: Signpost again, now at full force

stops.hear: The birdcall tune returns, now on the cor anglais, two octaves lower than the flute had it

stops.label: Last 45 seconds
stops.hear: The tempo presses on; brass and timpani drive to a short, fierce end

notice: Listen for the hymn each time it returns: at the start, at the start of the development, and at the climax in the trumpets. It tells you where you are in the movement.
The cor anglais plays only a few bars in the whole symphony. Wait for it in the recapitulation: the birdcall sounds darker and more tender in its low, reedy voice.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Kubelík, born in Bohemia, recorded the symphony with the Berlin Philharmonic in 1966 as part of his complete Dvořák cycle for Deutsche Grammophon. He is reported to have told an orchestra that in Bohemia the trumpets never call to battle: they call to the dance. On the Spotify album the symphony is tracks 1–4, followed by the Ninth, “From the New World”.

movements.heading: Adagio
movements.summary: A slow movement that keeps changing its mind. It opens in C minor with a hesitant phrase in the strings, answered by birdlike calls in the woodwinds. Then the sun comes out: a C major melody for flute and oboe over gently falling violin scales, taken up by a solo violin and then by the whole orchestra with brass fanfares. The dark music returns, a storm breaks out, and the movement ends in calm.

mainIdeas.name: The opening
mainIdeas.description: a soft, halting string phrase that stops and starts, as if unsure where to go.

mainIdeas.name: The birdcalls
mainIdeas.description: short falling figures in the flutes and oboes, answered by the clarinets.

mainIdeas.name: The C major tune
mainIdeas.description: a simple, swaying melody in flute and oboe over scales that trickle down in the violins.

stops.hear: Strings play a quiet, hesitant phrase that dies away
Flutes and oboes answer with little falling calls; clarinets reply
A sudden strong outburst in the strings
A calm, swaying tune in flute and oboe, while the violins trickle down a scale again and again
stops.happening: The C major section, the movement’s sunniest music

stops.hear: A solo violin sings the tune, high and sweet
stops.happening: The tune passed to one player

stops.hear: The whole orchestra plays the C major tune loudly; trumpets ring out a fanfare
The hesitant opening phrase returns
Full orchestra, loud and turbulent, with heavy brass

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The music settles; quiet woodwind calls and a soft close

notice: Many listeners hear a summer day in this movement, with birds, sunshine and a passing thunderstorm. Dvořák left no programme, so it is only one way to hear it, but the woodwind calls really do sound like birds.

movements.heading: Allegretto grazioso – Molto vivace
movements.summary: In place of a fast, joking [[scherzo|scherzo]], Dvořák writes a waltz: graceful, a little melancholy, in G minor. The middle section is a brighter folk-like tune in G major that he borrowed from his own comic opera *The Stubborn Lovers* (1874). At the end the tempo changes from three beats to two, and the borrowed tune rushes past in a quick dance.

mainIdeas.name: The waltz
mainIdeas.description: a sighing, gliding melody in the violins, in three beats.

mainIdeas.name: The trio tune
mainIdeas.description: a simple, swinging G major melody for flutes and oboes, later for oboe and bassoon.

stops.hear: The violins sing a graceful, slightly sad waltz
stops.happening: The main section, in G minor

stops.hear: The waltz grows warmer and fuller, with the whole string section
A brighter, rustic tune in flutes and oboes, over a gentle swaying accompaniment
stops.happening: The [[trio|trio]], in G major. The tune comes from the opera *The Stubborn Lovers*

stops.hear: The same tune in the oboe and bassoon
stops.happening: The trio repeated in a new colour

stops.hear: The waltz returns

stops.label: Last 45 seconds
stops.hear: Suddenly fast and in two beats: the trio tune races by

notice: At the very end the music switches from three beats to two. Notice how the gentle trio tune becomes a quick village dance just by changing its step.

movements.heading: Allegro ma non troppo
movements.summary: A trumpet fanfare, a silence, and then a quiet tune in the cellos. The rest of the movement is a set of [[variation|variation]]s on that tune, some fast, some slow, one in the minor like a stamping village band. The fanfare returns halfway through, a slow, tender variation follows, and the symphony ends in a blaze of brass and timpani.

mainIdeas.name: The theme
mainIdeas.description: a gentle, rocking tune in the cellos, which will be varied again and again.

mainIdeas.name: The village band
mainIdeas.description: a march-like section in C minor, with stamping rhythms and shrill woodwinds.

stops.hear: Two trumpets play a ringing fanfare, then a silence
The cellos play a quiet, rocking tune
The whole orchestra breaks in with the tune, faster and loud; horns trill above
A flute races up and down in quick notes
The music turns to the minor: stamping rhythms, shrill woodwinds, like a village band
stops.happening: The central variation, in C minor

stops.hear: The trumpet fanfare returns
Everything slows down; the theme sounds quiet and tender in the strings and woodwinds
The tempo picks up again and keeps accelerating

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: Brass and timpani blaze; the strings rush in sliding, chromatic runs to the final chords

notice: Count how many different characters the cellos’ tune takes on: gentle, triumphant, virtuosic, rustic, tender, wild. It is the same melody each time.

threads.title: Nature and birds
threads.body: The flute’s birdcall in the first movement, the woodwind calls in the Adagio and the flute’s flight in the finale: the countryside around Vysoká is heard throughout.

threads.title: Signposts
threads.body: The hymn of the first movement and the fanfare of the finale both come back to mark the start of a new section. Dvořák uses them to guide the ear through forms he treated freely.

threads.title: Song and dance
threads.body: Almost every theme could be sung, and many could be danced: the waltz, the borrowed opera tune, the village band. Dvořák’s love of Czech folk music shapes the whole symphony, though he quotes no actual folk song.
